lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: Welcome to JavaScript Engine Internals. Every time you write JavaScript, an engine is making thousands of decisions about your code, and most of us never look at them. We write a loop, we call a function, we add a property to an object, and somehow it runs fast. In this course we are going to open the box. The engine we will study is V8, the one inside Chrome and Node.js, and we will use Node because it lets us run tiny files from the terminal and ask V8 to tell us what it is doing. Nothing here is magic. Everything we cover, JIT compilation, hidden classes, deoptimization, garbage collection, is an engineering decision that you can read, measure and eventually predict.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: The way this course works is simple. We will not just talk about diagrams. For almost every idea I will write a small benchmark file, run it with a V8 flag, and read the output together. So you will see real bytecode printed by `node --print-bytecode`, real optimization events from `--trace-opt`, real bailouts from `--trace-deopt`, and a real profile from `--prof`. Those four flags are our instruments, and by the end you will be comfortable reading all of them.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: Let me tell you the path. We begin with the pipeline: what happens between your source text and a running program. Then we look at parsing, including lazy parsing, which is V8's first big optimization. After that we meet Ignition, the bytecode interpreter, and learn to read its output. Then TurboFan, the optimizing JIT compiler, and the idea of type feedback and speculation. We follow that with hidden classes and inline caches, which is how V8 makes property access cheap. Then the garbage collector, young generation and old generation. And finally we pull everything together into practical, V8-friendly code.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: Why does this matter for you as a working developer? Because performance cliffs are real. A function that is fast in one version of your code can become many times slower after an innocent change, like adding a property in a different order or passing a string where a number used to go. If you only know the surface language, that looks random. If you know what the engine is doing, it becomes a thing you can reason about and fix. Let me also say what this course is not. It is not a list of micro-optimization tricks to sprinkle on your code. In fact I will argue the opposite many times: write clear code first, measure, and only then use what you know about V8 to explain what you measured. The engine team changes internals constantly, so I will teach you the stable ideas and show you how to verify details yourself with the flags, instead of asking you to memorize specifics.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: For the demos you only need a recent version of Node installed and a terminal. I will use a few small files throughout: `add.js` for bytecode, `hot.js` for optimization, `deopt.js` for bailouts, `shapes.js` for hidden classes, `gc.js` for memory, and `prof.js` for profiling. I will tell you each time we create one, so you can follow along file by file. In the next lecture we start where every program starts, with a string of source text, and we ask what V8 has to do before a single line can run. Let's go.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: A quick word on how to get the most from each lecture. Pause when I run a command and run it yourself, even if you think you know what will happen. The point of these flags is that the output is surprising often enough to teach you something. When your output differs from mine, that is not a mistake, it is data. Different Node versions ship different V8 versions, and V8 changes its heuristics, so thresholds and message formats drift. I will always explain the concept first, so a slightly different log line will still make sense to you. One more thing. Throughout the course I will ask you to predict before I run. Will this function be optimized? Will this call cause a bailout? Prediction is the skill we are really building. Anyone can read a log after the fact. The goal is that, looking at a piece of code, you develop a feel for which stage of the pipeline it lives in and what V8 is probably thinking about it.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: Let's start with a question that sounds almost silly. When you type `node app.js` and hit enter, what actually happens to your code? We call JavaScript an interpreted language, but that word hides a lot. Your file is just text. A processor cannot run text. It runs machine instructions. So somewhere between the characters you typed and the instructions on the chip, a translation has to occur, and V8 does that translation in stages. Here is the shape of it, and we will spend the whole course filling in the details. First, V8 reads your source and turns it into tokens, then into a tree that represents the structure of the program. That tree is called the abstract syntax tree. Second, a bytecode generator walks that tree and produces compact instructions for an interpreter called Ignition. Third, while the bytecode runs, V8 watches which functions are hot, meaning called often, and hands those to an optimizing compiler called TurboFan, which generates real machine code.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: Notice something important about that design. V8 does not compile everything as hard as it can up front. Optimizing compilers are expensive, and most code in a typical page or server runs only once, during startup. So V8 starts cheap and gets smarter only where it pays off. That trade, start fast and optimize the hot parts, is the heart of every modern JavaScript engine. I want you to hold a mental picture of two speeds. The interpreter is quick to start but slow per instruction. The optimizing compiler is slow to start, because it needs time and information, but the code it produces is fast. V8 moves a function from the first world to the second only when evidence says it is worth it. We will call that evidence feedback, and it is a theme for the entire course.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: There is one more piece running beside all of this, and that is memory management. Every object, array and closure you create lives on a heap, and you never free it yourself. The garbage collector does that, and it runs alongside your code, sometimes in parallel threads, trying not to pause you. We have a whole chapter on it later. So when somebody says JavaScript is slow or fast, the honest answer is: it depends which stage your code is in. A function in its first call is in the interpreter. The same function after ten thousand calls may be machine code. And if you break an assumption, it can fall back down again. That falling back is called deoptimization, and it will explain many mysteries.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What Happens When You Run JavaScript
text: Let me put this in one sentence you can remember: parse, interpret, observe, optimize, and if you were wrong, bail out and repeat. In the next lecture we draw the full pipeline with its names, and then we start running real commands. Before we leave this overview, one practical thought. Because of this staged design, the first run of your code and the millionth run of your code can behave very differently. That is why benchmarks that time a single call tell you almost nothing. A fair measurement needs warm-up, so the engine can reach steady state. We will keep that in mind every time we measure something in this course, and I will remind you when a result is only valid after warm-up.

Now let's name the parts properly, because the names will show up in flags, in logs and in blog posts you read later. The input is your source code. The first component is the parser, which includes a scanner that produces tokens. The parser output is the abstract syntax tree, often shortened to AST. That tree goes to the bytecode generator, and the bytecode runs on Ignition, V8's interpreter. While Ignition executes, it does something quietly clever. For each function it keeps a structure called a feedback vector. Every time an operation runs, like an addition or a property load, V8 records what kinds of values it saw there. Was it always small integers? Always objects with the same layout? That record is the raw material the optimizer will use.

When a function gets hot enough, V8 passes the bytecode and that feedback to TurboFan. TurboFan builds a graph representation, applies optimizations based on the types it observed, and emits machine code for your actual processor. That machine code is guarded. At the points where it assumed something, such as this value is always an integer, it includes a quick check. If the check fails, execution drops back to the interpreter. That drop is the deoptimization. Recent versions of V8 have added extra tiers between those two. There is a baseline compiler called Sparkplug that quickly turns bytecode into unoptimized machine code, and a mid tier called Maglev in newer releases. I mention them so the names do not surprise you. But the mental model of interpreter, then optimizing compiler, with feedback in between, stays true, and the exact tiers can differ between Node versions. When it matters I will tell you how to check your own version.

Off to the side there is the heap and the garbage collector. Objects live in different regions, a small young generation where most things die quickly, and a larger old generation for survivors. The collector for the young region is called the scavenger, and the one for the old region uses a mark, sweep and compact approach. Let me summarize the pipeline in a way you can sketch on paper. Source, then parser, then AST, then bytecode, then Ignition, with feedback flowing into TurboFan, which produces optimized code, with an arrow back from optimized code to Ignition labeled deopt. Draw that once by hand tonight. Every lecture from here is zooming into one of those boxes, and having the picture in your head will keep you oriented.

Let me give you a small habit that pays off immediately. Whenever you read about V8 performance, ask which box in the diagram the claim is about. Is it about parsing cost, interpreter speed, optimized code quality, or memory? Many arguments online are really two people talking about different boxes. If you can place the claim on the diagram, you can usually tell whether it applies to your situation, and that is a skill we will practice constantly.

It also helps to know where each of these boxes shows up when something goes wrong. A syntax error is the parser complaining, and it happens before any of your code runs. A function that is slow only the first time is paying for compilation. A function that is fast for a while and then suddenly slow is probably a deoptimization. A program whose memory climbs and then drops in a sawtooth is garbage collection doing its job. Each symptom points at a stage, and that is why the pipeline picture is so useful for debugging. Let me also set expectations about what you can control. You cannot tell V8 to optimize a function, at least not in ordinary code. What you can do is write code whose shape is predictable, so that the feedback V8 collects is clean and the optimized code it produces stays valid. Everything in the final chapter is about that. The engine does the heavy lifting, and you are just making its job easier.

Time to get our hands dirty. Open a terminal and check your Node version with `node --version`. Any reasonably recent version will do, though the exact output of some flags changes between versions, so if yours differs slightly from mine, don't worry, the ideas hold. Create a new folder called `v8-lab` and move into it. Everything in this course lives in that folder. Our first file is called `add.js`. Inside I write a function: `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`. Then below it I call it once, `console.log(add(1, 2));`. Run it with `node add.js` and you see 3. Nothing special. Now here is the trick. Node passes unknown flags straight to V8, so we can run `node --print-bytecode add.js` and V8 will dump the bytecode it generates for every function it compiles.

You will see a wall of output, and that is normal, because Node itself is written partly in JavaScript and V8 prints bytecode for all of that too. To cut through it, add a filter: `node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=add add.js`. Now you only see the bytecode for the function named add. We will read it line by line in a later chapter, but notice the small size. A one-line function becomes just a few instructions. Second flag: `--trace-opt`. For that I make a new file, `hot.js`. It has the same add function, then a loop that calls it a few hundred thousand times with numbers, summing the results into a variable and printing it at the end. Run `node --trace-opt hot.js`. When the function gets hot, V8 prints lines saying it is marking the function for optimization and then compiling it. Those lines are your proof that the JIT is working.

Third flag, `--trace-deopt`. We will use it with a file called `deopt.js`, which calls add with numbers for a long while and then suddenly with strings. Run it and you should see V8 print a bailout message with a reason. We will decode that message later in the course. For now I just want you to see that the engine tells you, plainly, when it changes its mind. Fourth is `--prof`, which writes a log file you process afterwards with `node --prof-process`. That one gets its own lecture at the end. Keep the four flags in a notes file: print-bytecode, trace-opt, trace-deopt, prof. Those are our instruments. Next chapter we begin at the front of the pipeline, with tokenization.

One last setup tip. When you start experimenting, keep each demo file tiny and run it in isolation. Big programs trigger so many compilations that the logs become unreadable. A twenty-line file that does exactly one thing is the best microscope you have. And remember these flags are for learning and diagnosing, not for production. Leave them out of your real start scripts. Also, if a flag is not recognized in your version, run `node --v8-options` to list everything your build supports, which is a handy way to discover what else V8 can tell you.

Let me do a quick sanity run so you can confirm your setup matches mine. In `v8-lab`, run `node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=add add.js` and look for a block that starts with the function name and a few lines of numbered instructions. If you see it, your Node and V8 are ready. If you see nothing, check that the filter name matches your function name exactly, because the filter is a plain name match. Also try running `node --trace-opt hot.js | head` to see the first few optimization events without drowning in lines. If both work, you are done with setup, and I will see you in the next chapter.

Welcome to chapter two, where we go to the very front of the pipeline. Before V8 can do anything clever with your program, it has to understand it, and understanding starts with reading characters. In this lecture we look at tokenization, which in V8 is done by a component called the scanner. Its job is to take the raw text of your file and chop it into the smallest meaningful pieces, called tokens. By the end you should be able to look at any line of code and imagine it split the way the engine splits it, which sounds trivial but explains a lot of syntax rules.

Think about this line from our `add.js` file: `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`. To you it is one tidy line. To the scanner it is a stream of characters, and it has to decide where each word ends. It produces roughly this sequence: the keyword `function`, an identifier `add`, a left parenthesis, the identifier `a`, a comma, the identifier `b`, a right parenthesis, a left brace, the keyword `return`, the identifier `a`, a plus sign, the identifier `b`, a semicolon, and a right brace. Whitespace and comments are skipped. They matter to humans and not to the machine.

Each token has a type, and sometimes a value. The identifier token carries the name. A number token carries the number. A string token carries the contents. Keywords like `function` and `return` are recognized by looking the identifier up in a table, so the scanner can tell a variable called `returnValue` apart from the keyword `return`. Scanning is fast, because it is a simple loop over characters with a lot of small decisions, and V8 has optimized it heavily, including special handling for plain ASCII text. Now, why should you care? Because the scanner is where some surprising costs hide. Very long files take longer to scan. Heavy use of comments costs little, but they are still read. Minifiers shorten names and strip whitespace partly to reduce download size, and also to reduce the work at this stage. Another subtle thing: the scanner must handle tricky cases like regular expression literals versus division. The slash character means different things depending on what came before it, so the scanner and parser cooperate there.

Template literals are another good example. When you write a backtick string with a dollar-brace expression inside, the scanner has to switch modes, scan the string part, pause for the embedded expression, and then resume the string. Automatic semicolon insertion is similar. The rules that let you leave off semicolons are applied by the parser using information about line breaks that the scanner records, which is why a line break right after `return` changes what your code means. Let me connect this to something you can observe. Make a file called `lex.js` with a deliberate typo, like an unterminated string. Run it with `node lex.js`. You get a SyntaxError, and notice nothing from your program ran at all, not even an earlier console.log. That is because the whole file has to be scanned and parsed before execution begins. A syntax error is caught up front, and the engine never starts your program.

One more point before we move on. Tokens are not kept around forever. The scanner produces them on demand as the parser asks for the next one, so V8 does not build a giant list of tokens in memory first. It reads a token, the parser consumes it, and the scanner moves on. That streaming design keeps memory low and is part of why parsing can start before a script has even finished downloading in the browser. In the next lecture we take that stream of tokens and watch it become a tree, the abstract syntax tree, which is the structure everything after this stage is built from.

Last time the scanner gave us a stream of tokens. A flat stream is not enough, though. Consider `a + b * c`. The tokens alone do not tell you that the multiplication happens first. For that you need structure, and the structure V8 builds is called the abstract syntax tree, or AST. In this lecture we look at what it is, why it is abstract, and what V8 does with it. The parser reads tokens and checks them against the grammar of JavaScript. As it recognizes a construct, it creates a node. For our add function, the root is a function literal node. Inside it is a parameter list with two names, and a body containing a return statement. The return statement has one child, a binary operation node for the plus sign, and that node has two children, the variable `a` and the variable `b`. That is the tree. Nested things become children of the things that contain them.

Why abstract? Because the tree throws away details that were only needed for reading the text. The parentheses around an expression are gone, since the shape of the tree already says what groups with what. Semicolons are gone. Whitespace is gone. What remains is the meaning of the program, not how it was typed. Two differently formatted versions of the same function produce the same tree. You can look at an AST yourself, even though V8's own is internal. Tools like Acorn or the parser used by many editors produce similar trees in JSON. Paste `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }` into one and you will see a node of type function, a body of type block, and a return statement with a binary expression. V8 has its own node classes in C++, but the idea is identical, and looking at a friendly version is a great way to build intuition.

The parser does one more important job while building the tree: scope analysis. For every variable it must decide where it lives. Is it a parameter? A local? A variable from an outer function that a closure captures? Those answers decide whether the variable can sit in a register, or has to be stored in a heap-allocated context so that an inner function can reach it later. We will see the effect of that decision in the bytecode, because registers and context slots look different there. After parsing, the AST goes to the bytecode generator, which walks the tree and emits instructions. For `a + b` it visits the left child, then the right child, then emits an add. A tree maps very naturally to that kind of walk. Once the bytecode exists, V8 no longer needs the tree for that function, and the memory can be reclaimed. That detail matters, because it means the AST is a temporary structure and keeping it alive is not free.

Here is the takeaway I want you to hold. The tokens tell V8 what words are there, the AST tells it what they mean together, and the bytecode tells it what to do. Each stage is a step toward something executable. Next, we look at why V8 does not build a full tree for every function in your program, and the answer is one of its most effective tricks, lazy parsing. Let me suggest a small exercise. Take a function you wrote recently and sketch its tree on paper. Start with the function node, then its parameters, then the body, and nest each statement and expression underneath. Do it for something with an if statement and a loop. You will notice that every construct becomes a node with a fixed set of children, and that makes the later stages mechanical. I do this when I am confused about operator precedence, and it settles the question every time.

Here is a thought experiment. A typical web application ships hundreds of kilobytes of JavaScript. How much of it runs during startup? Usually only a fraction. There are error handlers that never fire, features behind menus nobody opened yet, and library code for cases you do not use. If V8 fully parsed and compiled every function in every file before running anything, you would pay for a lot of work that never mattered. So V8 does not do that. This is lazy parsing, and it is V8's first big optimization.

The idea is simple. When V8 meets a function declaration, it does a quick pass called preparsing. The preparser scans through the function body just far enough to check that the syntax is valid and to find where the function ends, and to learn which outer variables it uses. It does not build a full AST and it does not generate bytecode. Later, if the function is actually called, V8 goes back and does the full parse and compile at that moment. Pay attention to that word, deferred, because it is the key to why startup stays fast even when a bundle is enormous.

Let me show it. Create a file called `lazy.js` with a function `function unused() { /* large body */ }` that is never called, and a function `function used() { return 1; }` that is called once at the bottom. Run `node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=used lazy.js` and you will see bytecode for `used`. Change the filter to `unused` and you get nothing, because the function was never compiled. That is lazy compilation made visible. Now add a call to `unused()` at the bottom and run it again, and the bytecode for it appears, which is the proof that compilation happens at first call.

There is a cost to this, and it is worth understanding. If a function is called, V8 has effectively scanned it twice, once for the preparse and once for the full parse. For code that you know runs immediately, that is wasted effort. V8 uses a heuristic: if a function is wrapped in parentheses, like an immediately invoked function expression, it guesses you are about to call it and compiles it eagerly. That is why you may see module bundlers wrap code in parentheses. Treat it as a hint rather than a guarantee, and do not sprinkle parentheses everywhere without measuring.

Inner functions add a twist. When the preparser skips an inner function, it must still record which outer variables the inner function references, since those variables may need to live in a heap context instead of a register. The preparser tracks exactly that. It is a middle path, cheaper than a full parse but not free, and V8 engineers keep working to make it faster. There is also caching. Chrome and Node can store compiled bytecode in a code cache so that the next run skips parsing and compiling for scripts that did not change. In Node you can use the `v8-compile-cache` approach or the built-in compile cache support in newer versions. Startup of a big command-line tool can improve noticeably with it. Again, the principle is the same: do work only when needed, and do it only once.

So what does this mean for your code? Mostly, relax. Lazy parsing works in your favor automatically. Keep code you do not need at startup out of the startup path, use dynamic imports to defer whole modules, and do not worry about unused functions in a file. In the next chapter we leave the front end and meet what the parser feeds, Ignition and its bytecode.

We have a tree. Now what? You could in principle execute a tree directly by walking it, and some simple interpreters do. But V8 made a different choice: it turns the tree into bytecode. In this lecture we look at what bytecode is and why V8 bothers with this extra step. The interpreter that runs it is called Ignition. Bytecode is a list of small, simple instructions for a virtual machine, a made-up processor that exists only inside V8. Each instruction has an opcode, which says what to do, and operands, which say what to do it with. It is called bytecode because each opcode fits in one byte. It is much lower level than your source, since there are no nested expressions anymore, just a flat sequence of steps. But it is much higher level than real machine code, because it does not know about your particular processor, whether it is Intel or ARM.

Why not skip bytecode and compile straight to machine code? The answer is memory and startup. Early V8 compiled everything directly to machine code, and on phones that cost a lot of memory, because machine code is bulky and most of it never ran. Bytecode is far more compact. The Ignition project, which landed in V8 several years ago, cut memory use noticeably and also made startup faster, since generating bytecode is cheap. There is a second reason, and it is more important for this course. Bytecode gives V8 one clean, uniform representation of your function that everything else builds on. Ignition interprets it. The optimizing compiler reads it as its input, together with type feedback. When V8 deoptimizes, it needs a place to go back to, and that place is a position in the bytecode. One format serves all those purposes, which keeps the engine simpler and much easier to keep correct.

Bytecode also makes V8 portable. The code that generates bytecode is the same on every platform. Only the part that executes it, and the part that generates machine code later, differs by architecture. That is a big deal for an engine that runs on desktops, servers, phones and embedded devices. Let me show you the real thing. In your `v8-lab` folder, open `add.js` again and run `node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=add add.js`. You will see a short header, with a parameter count, a register count and a frame size, and then a few lines, each starting with an address and then a mnemonic. We will decode those in the next lecture. For now just notice: three or so instructions for a one-line function. That is how small and regular this format is.

Now imagine you have a thousand functions. Storing bytecode for each is cheap. Storing optimized machine code for each would be expensive, so V8 only does that for the hot ones. That is the economy of the whole design, and Ignition is its foundation. Next we learn to read these instructions one at a time. One more benefit of a bytecode design is that it makes tooling possible. Because the instruction stream is well defined, V8 can print it, as we just did, and developers on the V8 team can debug the compiler pipeline by reading it. When you file or read a V8 bug report, bytecode listings are often attached. Learning to read them is a bit like learning to read assembly for a friendly processor, and it pays off whenever you wonder why a piece of code behaves the way it does.

There is also a trade-off, and I want to be honest about it. An interpreter running bytecode is slower than machine code, because every instruction has to be fetched, decoded and dispatched. Ignition mitigates this with carefully hand-tuned handlers for each bytecode, but it is still the slow tier. That is exactly why the optimizing compiler exists, to take the functions that run a lot and replace this interpretation with direct machine code.

Let's read some bytecode. Run `node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=add add.js` with the file we made earlier. You will see a header first. It says something like parameter count 3, register count 0, and a frame size. Parameter count is three even though add has two parameters, because the receiver, the value of `this`, counts as one. The exact header layout can vary between Node versions, so focus on the instructions underneath. For `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }` the body looks like this. First, `Ldar a1`. Then `Add a0, [0]`. Then `Return`. Three instructions. Let's go through them. The mnemonic `Ldar` means load accumulator from register. Here the register is `a1`, which is the second argument, `b`. So after this instruction, the value of `b` is sitting in the accumulator. We will explain the accumulator properly in the next lecture, but think of it as a special working register.

Next is `Add a0, [0]`. This adds the value in register `a0`, which is our first argument `a`, to the value already in the accumulator, and leaves the result in the accumulator. The number in square brackets is the feedback slot index. It tells the interpreter which slot in the feedback vector to use to record the types it observes at this addition. That little bracketed number is how type feedback is wired in, and it is the thing the optimizer will read later. The last instruction, `Return`, ends the function and returns whatever is in the accumulator. That is the whole function. Notice how the order is a bit surprising. We loaded `b` first and then added `a`. That is because the add instruction takes one operand from a register and the other from the accumulator, so the generator chooses an order that fits. Do not worry about it. Just remember the pattern.

Let me try a slightly bigger one. In the same file, add `function twice(x) { let y = x + 1; return y * 2; }` and call it. Print its bytecode with the filter set to `twice`. You will see `LdaSmi [1]`, which loads the small integer one into the accumulator. Then an `Add` using the register that holds `x`. Then a `Star` instruction, which stores the accumulator into a register for `y`. Then `LdaSmi [2]`, a `Mul` and a `Return`. Newer Node versions print the short forms like `Star0` and `Star1`, older ones print `Star r0`. Same thing.

Here is a vocabulary tip. Most mnemonics follow a pattern. Anything starting with `Lda` loads into the accumulator. Anything starting with `Sta` or `Star` stores from the accumulator. `Ldar` and `Star` move between accumulator and registers. Arithmetic like `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul` works with the accumulator. Jumps like `Jump` and `JumpIfFalse` control flow, and `JumpLoop` closes a loop. Calls use mnemonics beginning with `Call`. Once you know the pattern, unfamiliar bytecode stops looking scary. Try this yourself before the next lecture. Write a loop that sums numbers from one to ten, print its bytecode, and find the `JumpLoop` at the end. Seeing your own source reflected in these instructions is the best way to get fluent.

A practical note about the filter flag. The filter matches function names, so for anonymous arrow functions assigned to a variable, V8 usually infers the variable name and prints it. Top-level script code appears under a name like the main function of the script, and you may also see lots of other output if you leave the filter off. If your output looks empty, check your spelling first, and then check that the function was actually called, because lazy compilation means an uncalled function never gets bytecode at all. Also, do not memorize mnemonics. The list changes as V8 evolves, and engineers add new instructions to speed up common patterns. What matters is that you can read a listing, spot loads, stores, arithmetic, calls and jumps, and connect them back to your source. When you meet a mnemonic you do not know, a quick search of the V8 source for its name, or just guessing from the name, usually gets you there.

In the last lecture I promised to explain the accumulator, and this is where we do it. Ignition is what is called a register machine with an accumulator. That description tells you a lot about how the bytecode is shaped, so let's unpack it. There are two kinds of storage. First, registers. Each function gets a numbered set of virtual registers, named r0, r1, and so on, which hold local variables and temporary values. Function arguments live in registers too, named a0, a1 and so on. These are not real CPU registers. They are slots in the function's stack frame. Second, there is one special register called the accumulator, which is implicit. Most instructions use it without even naming it.

Why have an accumulator at all? Because it makes bytecode smaller. If every addition had to say add this register to that register and put the result in a third register, each instruction would need three operands. With an accumulator, many instructions need only one explicit operand, and the other input and the output are implicitly the accumulator. Fewer operands means fewer bytes, and fewer bytes means a more compact function that is faster to fetch and uses less memory. That is a direct payoff of the design.

Let's trace a small example by hand. Suppose we have `function calc(a, b) { let c = a + b; return c * 2; }`. The generator might produce this. `Ldar a1` loads b into the accumulator. `Add a0, [0]` adds a, leaving the sum in the accumulator. `Star0` stores the accumulator into r0, which is our variable `c`. Then `LdaSmi [2]` puts the integer two into the accumulator. `Mul r0, [1]` multiplies r0 by the accumulator. `Return` returns the accumulator. Follow the value in the accumulator line by line and you can simulate the whole function. The register count in the header now makes sense. For `calc` it would say one register, because we have one local, `c`. For `add` it said zero, since nothing needed a temporary. Registers are allocated by the bytecode generator, which tries to reuse them, so a function with many temporaries does not always have a long register list.

A quick word about small integers. The mnemonic `LdaSmi` stands for load small integer, with Smi short for small integer. V8 represents small whole numbers directly inside a tagged value rather than as heap objects, so loading one is nearly free. Larger numbers and fractions are stored as heap numbers, which are allocated objects. That difference will matter a lot when we reach optimization, because integer arithmetic on Smis is one of the cheapest things the engine does. Let's recap the chapter. Source becomes a tree, the tree becomes bytecode, and Ignition runs bytecode on a register machine with an accumulator, recording feedback in numbered slots as it goes. That feedback is what the next chapter is built on. We will see what TurboFan does when it reads it, and what happens when the data it relied on stops being true.

To make this concrete, run this experiment. In a new file, write a function with a handful of local variables and some arithmetic between them, then print its bytecode and count the registers in the header. Now rewrite the function to reuse a single variable instead of several, and print again. You will often see the register count drop. It is a nice way to see that the shape of your source influences what the generator emits, even though the difference rarely matters for speed on its own.

I also want to flag a misconception. People sometimes assume the accumulator is a performance trick on its own. It is not. It is mainly a size trick, with a speed side effect, because in the interpreter the accumulator can be kept in a real CPU register while the handler runs. So the design is small and fast to dispatch. When TurboFan later takes over, all this register and accumulator machinery disappears, and the optimizer builds its own representation from the bytecode. The virtual machine is only the starting point.

Welcome to the TurboFan chapter. So far we have been in the interpreter, and the interpreter is the slow tier. In this lecture we meet the idea that makes JavaScript fast enough for serious work: just-in-time compilation, or JIT. Let's define it, and then see it happen. A traditional compiler, like one for C, translates your whole program to machine code before it ever runs. That is ahead-of-time compilation. A JIT compiler does the translation while the program is running, on the fly, only for the code that turns out to matter. That is a huge advantage for a language like JavaScript, because the engine does not know in advance which functions will be hot, and it can actually watch the program and decide.

The watching is done by Ignition. As functions run, V8 counts how often they are called and how many loop iterations they execute. When a function crosses a threshold and its behavior looks stable, V8 marks it for optimization and sends it to TurboFan, V8's optimizing compiler. TurboFan compiles it to machine code, often on a background thread so your program keeps running while the compile is in progress. When it finishes, the next call to that function jumps straight into the optimized code. Let's see it live. Open `hot.js`, which has our add function and a loop that calls it, say, one million times with numbers. Run `node --trace-opt hot.js`. Among the output you will see lines that mention marking the function for optimization, then compiling it with TurboFan, and then completing the compile. The messages vary between versions, and newer ones mention the tier and a reason like the function being hot and stable. That sequence is the JIT doing its job.

Why does optimized code run faster? Several reasons. It is real machine code, so there is no instruction dispatch. TurboFan can inline small functions into their callers, so the call overhead disappears. It can keep values in real CPU registers instead of stack slots. It can remove checks and repeated work it can prove are unnecessary. And most importantly, it can make assumptions based on what the feedback says, which leads to our next topic. There is also a cost side. Compilation takes CPU time, and optimized code takes memory. That is the reason for the thresholds. If V8 optimized everything immediately, startup would be slower, not faster, and most of that work would be wasted. The system is a bet: spend compile time on code that will repay it. And there is no promise it will be optimized. A function called twice never will be, and that is exactly right.

In recent Node versions there are extra stages in between, like the baseline compiler and the mid tier I mentioned earlier. They exist to fill the gap, giving a cheaper speedup before the full optimizer kicks in. The shape of the story does not change: more heat, more optimization. Next lecture we look at the secret ingredient that lets TurboFan make bold assumptions, which is type feedback and speculation. Let me add one observation about how to read the trace-opt output without getting lost. Each line carries a function name and a memory address in angle brackets. Ignore the address. Find the function name, and then follow the sequence for that name: marked, compiled, completed. If a function name appears with a later line about being deoptimized, you have found a story worth investigating. For a first pass, grep the output for your own function names, because Node's internal functions will also appear.

Also remember the loop case. A function called only once, but containing a very hot loop, can be optimized in the middle of running, through a technique called on-stack replacement. V8 swaps the running interpreter frame for an optimized one while the loop is still going. That is why a big loop at the top level of a script can still get fast, even though the surrounding code ran only once.

JavaScript is dynamically typed. In `a + b`, the values could be numbers, strings, objects, or anything. That is a nightmare for a compiler that wants to emit one fast machine instruction. If it had to handle every possible type, the code would be bloated with checks and branches. So how does TurboFan produce fast code for a language with no types? It cheats, in a principled way, and it is called speculation. Remember the feedback vector we met in the bytecode lecture? That bracketed number after `Add a0, [0]` points at a slot. Each time the addition runs in Ignition, V8 records in that slot the kinds of operands it saw. Small integers only? Then the slot says so. Numbers with fractions too? The slot generalizes. Strings seen? It generalizes again. The slot only moves from specific to general, never back, so it is a summary of everything that ever happened at that site.

Now TurboFan reads those slots when it compiles. If the addition in `add` has only ever seen small integers, TurboFan speculates that it will always see small integers. It generates a very fast integer addition, with a guard in front of it that checks that both inputs really are small integers, and a check for overflow. If the guard passes, which it nearly always does, you get the speed of C. The guard costs almost nothing compared to what it saves. That is the bargain. Type feedback tells V8 what is likely, speculation uses it to generate fast code, and guards keep it safe. The code is not correct for all inputs, it is correct for the inputs it was told to expect, plus a safety net for everything else. The safety net is deoptimization, which is the next lecture.

Let me show the effect with a benchmark. In `hot.js`, time a million calls to `add(i, 1)` with numbers only. Then in a second file, call it with a mix of numbers and strings for a while before the timed loop. You should see the mixed version run slower, because the feedback is no longer clean, and TurboFan has to generate more general code. Use `performance.now()` around the loop and run each a few times for stable numbers. Feedback is recorded for more than arithmetic. Property loads record the shapes of the objects they saw. Function calls record which function was called, which lets TurboFan inline it. Comparisons, array accesses, and many other operations all have slots. This is why consistency matters so much in V8 code, and we will see it again with hidden classes, because object shapes are the most important feedback of all.

One caution. Feedback is gathered only while code runs in the interpreter or baseline tiers. A function that is optimized very early may have seen only a narrow slice of inputs, such as the test data you used during startup. That is not a bug, it is how speculation works, but it explains why real-world input sometimes causes surprise bailouts. Real workloads are broader than your benchmark. So type feedback is the information, speculation is the bet, and guards are the insurance. Now let's cash the insurance and see what happens when a bet loses.

Let me give you an analogy that helped me. Imagine a cashier who has seen only ten dollar bills all morning. She starts handling them with a quick glance and no careful inspection, because the pattern is clear. If a foreign banknote arrives, she notices at the glance and stops to handle it the slow, careful way. That glance is the guard. The quick handling is the speculation. The slow careful way is the interpreter. It is a good deal as long as foreign banknotes are rare. This also explains a famous piece of advice: do not change the type of a variable. If a variable holds a number in one place and a string in another, the feedback at each site gets muddier, and the guards fail more often. Nothing breaks. You just lose the speculation advantage, and your code runs in the slower, more general mode.

Every bet can lose. What happens when optimized code meets a value it did not expect? It cannot just continue, because its machine code was built on the assumption that the guard protects. So V8 does something clever and important called deoptimization. The optimized code throws itself away and execution continues in the interpreter, as if the optimized version had never existed. Correctness is preserved, but speed is lost. Let's watch it. Open `deopt.js`. It has our add function, and then a loop that calls `add(i, 1)` for a few hundred thousand iterations with integers. That gets the function optimized. After that loop, I add one more call: `add('x', 'y')`, with strings. Now run it with `node --trace-opt --trace-deopt deopt.js`. First you see the function being optimized. Then, at the string call, you see a line starting with bailout or deoptimizing. It names the function, the reason, and where in the code it happened.

Read the reason carefully, because it is the whole diagnosis. For this case you will likely see a reason along the lines of not a Smi, meaning the guard expected a small integer and got something else. Other reasons you may meet are wrong map, which means an object had a different shape than expected, out of bounds for an array access beyond the length, or insufficient type feedback, when code ran that had never run before. The wording can shift between versions, but they all say: the assumption failed. What happens technically? The optimized code contains deoptimization points. Each point knows how to reconstruct the interpreter state, which bytecode position we were at and what values were in which registers, from the machine state at that moment. The deoptimizer rebuilds an interpreter frame and resumes in Ignition at the right instruction. The user never notices anything but a brief slowdown.

Deopts come in kinds. An eager deopt happens right at a failed guard. A lazy deopt happens when something else invalidates the optimized code, for instance a dependency on an object's shape that later changes, and the code is only discarded the next time it is entered. The log tells you which kind it was. After a deopt, the function goes back to the interpreter and starts collecting fresh feedback, now including the new type. Later it may be optimized again, this time with more general assumptions. If that cycle repeats, you can end up in a loop of optimize, bail out, optimize, bail out, and V8 eventually gives up on optimizing the function for a while. That pattern is the performance cliff people talk about.

So the practical lessons are these. Deoptimization is not an error, it is a safety mechanism. One deopt is cheap. Repeated deopts in hot code are expensive and show up clearly in `--trace-deopt`. And the way to avoid them is to keep the types at each site consistent. We will return to this in the final chapter with concrete patterns. First we need to cover how V8 handles objects, which is the next chapter. Let me show how to find the cause in practice. When you see a deopt in the log, note the function name and the reason. Open that function and look at the exact operation near the reported position. Ask what type the optimizer was expecting there, and then ask which caller could be supplying something different. Very often the culprit is not the function itself but a caller far away that passes an unusual value once. Logging the argument types at the call site, or searching for the one odd caller, usually finishes the investigation within minutes.

Here is a subtlety worth remembering. The same function can be optimized, deoptimized and reoptimized several times in a long-running server, and a handful of such cycles during warm-up is entirely normal. Do not chase every line in the log. Focus on functions that deoptimize repeatedly, or that are hot and show up in the profile, which is what we will learn to find with the profiler at the end of this course.

Welcome to chapter five, hidden classes and object shapes. This is where we answer a question that should bother you: how can `point.x` be fast? In a language like C, a struct field sits at a fixed offset, so reading it is one instruction. In JavaScript an object looks like a dictionary, where properties can be added and removed at any time. If V8 really did a dictionary lookup on every property access, JavaScript would be painfully slow. It does not, and here is how.

V8 gives every object a hidden description of its layout, called a hidden class. Inside V8 it is called a Map, which has nothing to do with the JavaScript Map collection, so do not mix them up. In other engines you may hear the names shape or structure. The idea is the same. The hidden class says: this object has properties named x and y, in this order, and x is stored at this offset, y at that offset. It is shared by every object with the same layout. Every object has a pointer to its hidden class in its header. When the code reads `point.x`, V8 can check the pointer against the expected hidden class, and if it matches, it knows exactly where x is. That is one comparison and one load, which is almost the same as the C struct. The expensive dictionary lookup is replaced by a cheap shape check. That is the whole trick, and it is why shape consistency matters so much to V8.

Let's look at the object layout in a bit more detail. An object has the hidden class pointer, a pointer to a properties store, a pointer to an elements store, and then a number of in-object property slots. When you create an object with a constructor or a literal, V8 usually reserves in-object space for the properties it expects, so the first several properties live right inside the object, and access is as fast as it gets. Extra properties that overflow go into an out-of-object properties array. Elements, meaning the integer-indexed values, are stored separately from named properties. That is why arrays and objects can both have indexed items without interfering with named fields. V8 further optimizes the kind of elements, tracking whether an array holds only small integers, only numbers, or arbitrary values, and it transitions between those kinds as you store different things. A packed array of small integers is much cheaper than a general one.

Now let me show you in code. Create `shapes.js`. I write `function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }`, then `const p1 = new Point(1, 2); const p2 = new Point(3, 4);`. Both objects were built by the same code, in the same order, so they share one hidden class. Run Node with the `--allow-natives-syntax` flag and call `%HaveSameMap(p1, p2)`. It prints true. The flag unlocks V8 internal functions with a percent sign prefix, and they are for experiments only, never for real code. So the takeaway: objects that are created the same way share a shape, and shared shape means fast property access. In the next lecture we see what happens when the creation order differs, and how V8 builds a tree of these shapes as properties get added.

Let me add a caution about names. Different articles call this thing a hidden class, a shape, a structure or a map, depending on the engine and the author. Inside V8's source it is a Map, and the debugging helper `%DebugPrint(p1)` prints the map address and its descriptors if you want to look at one directly. I will mostly say hidden class or shape, and I mean the same object each time.

How does an object get its hidden class in the first place? It starts empty, with an initial shape that has no properties. Every time you add a property, V8 does not mutate that shape, it moves the object to a different shape that includes the new property. That move is called a shape transition. And because many objects follow the same sequence, V8 can remember the transitions and reuse them. Stay with me, because the answer is one of the most elegant ideas in the whole engine.

Take `shapes.js` again and walk through `function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }`. A new Point starts with shape zero, the empty one. When `this.x = x` runs, V8 looks at the transition table of shape zero for a transition labeled x. The first time, there is none, so V8 creates a new shape, shape one, that has x, and records the link from shape zero to shape one on the label x. Then `this.y = y` does the same, creating shape two with x and y. The next Point you create finds both transitions already there and just follows them, with no new shapes.

So the shapes form a tree. The root is the empty shape, and each edge is a property addition. Two objects share a shape exactly when they followed the same path. That is the heart of this lecture, and it has a consequence you can test right now. Create `const a = {}; a.x = 1; a.y = 2;` and then `const b = {}; b.y = 2; b.x = 1;`. They have the same properties, but with the opposite order of addition, so they follow different branches of the tree and end up with different shapes. Check with `%HaveSameMap(a, b)` and you get false.

Does that matter? Yes, because remember that guards compare shapes. Code that handles both `a` and `b` sees two different shapes and its feedback gets more complicated. A function that sees one shape is monomorphic and fast. One that sees several is polymorphic and slower. We cover that in the next lecture on inline caches, and again in the final chapter. The practical rule that falls out is: initialize your properties in the same order, ideally all in the constructor. Object literals help here. When you write `{ x: 1, y: 2 }` in the same code location, V8 builds the object with the final shape in one go, based on a boilerplate for that literal, and so every execution of that literal produces objects with the same shape without walking transitions one by one. Literals with the same keys in the same order across different places in the code tend to end up with the same shape too.

What about removing properties? Using `delete obj.x` is a special case. In many situations it forces V8 to change the object into dictionary mode, sometimes called slow mode, where properties are stored in a hash table and the shape sharing goes away. Reads still work, but they are slower and harder to optimize. If you need to drop a property, setting it to `undefined` or `null` keeps the shape intact, and often is the better choice in performance-sensitive paths. Dictionary mode can also be triggered by adding a huge number of properties, or by using an object as a map with arbitrary keys. For that use case, prefer a real `Map`. So the transition tree is wonderful when objects look like records and not so great when they look like hash tables. Use each for what it is good at. Next lecture we take these shapes and see how V8 exploits them at the individual access site, through inline caches.

We have shapes. Now we need to know how code actually uses them, and the mechanism is the inline cache, or IC. Think about a line like `return p.x;` inside a function. Without any help, each time it runs V8 would have to look up where x lives for whatever object p is. Inline caches remember the answer at that particular site, so the next time is quick. Here is how it works. Every property access in your code has a feedback slot, the same kind we saw with addition. The first time the access runs, the slot is uninitialized, so V8 takes the slow path: it looks up x on the object's hidden class, finds its offset, and then records in the slot the pair of that hidden class and that offset. The second time, the access goes to the IC first, checks whether the object has the recorded hidden class, and if so just loads from the recorded offset. No lookup at all.

That state, where the site has seen exactly one shape, is called monomorphic. It is the best state. If the site later sees a second shape, the IC moves to polymorphic and stores a small list of shape and offset pairs, up to a handful of them. Access is a bit slower, since it has to compare against several shapes, but it is still fast. If the site sees too many different shapes, it goes megamorphic. Then V8 stops caching per site and falls back on a global lookup cache or the generic path. That is much slower, and optimized code cannot specialize on it.

Let's make this concrete with `shapes.js`. Write `function getX(p) { return p.x; }`. Call it in a loop with objects that all come from the Point constructor. This site is monomorphic. Now build a second kind of object, say `{ y: 2, x: 1 }` made in a different order, and mix them into the same loop. The site becomes polymorphic. Build six or seven different shapes, all with an x property, and the site becomes megamorphic. Time each loop with `performance.now()` and you will see the cost climb as the shape count grows. You can also peek at the state if you want. Recent Node versions support flags such as `--log-ic` which write IC events to a log, and older ones used `--trace-ic`. The flag names have moved around over time, so check `node --v8-options` for what your build offers. Reading these logs is an advanced skill. For this course the timing experiment is more than enough to make the point.

Why does all this matter to TurboFan? Because the feedback in those slots is exactly what it reads. A monomorphic site lets TurboFan emit one shape check and one direct load, and then further optimize with the knowledge of what the object looks like, even removing the load if it can prove the value. A polymorphic site gets a short switch. A megamorphic site gets a generic call into the runtime, and the optimization chain stops there. So the chain is complete. Same creation order gives the same shape. The same shape gives a monomorphic inline cache. A monomorphic cache gives tight optimized code. Break any link, and you slow down. In the next chapter we turn to memory and the garbage collector, because the objects we have been creating all have to live somewhere, and be cleaned up eventually.

A good habit to build is to ask, at any property access in hot code, how many shapes could reach it. If the answer is one, you are in the best case. If the answer is a small number, you are fine. If the answer is that it takes anything at all, such as a generic utility function called from everywhere with every kind of object, that site is probably megamorphic, and it is worth knowing about it even if you decide to leave it. Utility functions are the classic trap. A helper like `getName(obj)` used by dozens of unrelated types accumulates every shape in the program in its one inline cache, and then it is megamorphic for everybody. The standard remedy is not to avoid helpers, but to keep hot paths on a small, uniform set of object types, for example by having separate helpers for separate kinds of object.

Welcome to the memory chapter. Everything we have created so far, the objects, arrays, closures, and even the bytecode and the feedback vectors, lives on the V8 heap. In JavaScript you never free memory yourself, so something else must, and that something is the garbage collector. To understand it, we first need to see how the heap is laid out. V8 splits the heap into regions called spaces, because different kinds of data have different lifetimes. The most important split is between the young generation and the old generation. This design rests on an observation called the generational hypothesis: most objects die young. Think of the temporary objects you create inside a function, an options object, a result array, a string made for a log message. Within moments of creation they are garbage. A small number of objects, like your cache or your application state, live for a very long time.

So the young generation, also called new space, is a small region where every new object is allocated. Allocation there is extremely cheap, basically bumping a pointer forward. The new space is divided into two halves called semi-spaces, one active and one empty, and we will see why in the next lecture. When it fills up, a quick collection runs. Objects that survive a couple of those collections get promoted into the old generation, or old space, which is much larger and collected less often. There are other spaces too. The large object space holds objects too big for regular pages, like a huge array or buffer, so they are never copied around. The code space holds machine code generated by the compilers. Depending on your V8 version there may also be spaces for maps and other special data. You do not need to memorize them. The important picture is: small young area, big old area, plus special areas for big and special things.

You can see all this in action with a file we will call `gc.js`. It allocates many short-lived objects in a loop, for example creating an array of ten small objects a few hundred thousand times and discarding them. Run it with `node --trace-gc gc.js`. For every collection V8 prints a line. You will see lines labeled Scavenge, which are minor collections of the young generation, along with heap sizes before and after and the time spent. In a short run like this, most lines will say Scavenge. Read one of those lines slowly. It shows something like the used memory before, the used memory after, the total size, and a duration in milliseconds. Notice how the used memory drops sharply after each scavenge, since the garbage is gone. That sawtooth is what a healthy allocation-heavy program looks like.

Two knobs are worth knowing about. The flag `--max-old-space-size` sets the maximum size of the old generation in megabytes, and it is the one you reach for when a Node process runs out of memory. The flag `--max-semi-space-size` affects the size of the young generation, and a larger one can reduce promotion for allocation-heavy servers. We will only use them for experiments here. In the next lecture we zoom into the young generation and see exactly how a scavenge works. One practical habit: when you suspect a memory problem in Node, do not guess. Start with `--trace-gc` to see whether the heap keeps growing after major collections. If the used size after each Mark-Compact keeps climbing, something is being retained. If it returns to a stable level, you have allocation pressure but not a leak. That one distinction saves hours, because the fixes are completely different, one about holding on to less, the other about allocating less.

Also, `--expose-gc` lets you call `global.gc()` in an experiment to force a collection and compare numbers before and after. Use it for demos and tests only. In real programs, forcing collection is almost always a mistake, because V8 knows better than you when the right time is.

Let's look at the minor collector. In V8 it is called the scavenger, and its job is to clean the young generation quickly and often. The word quickly is the key. Because it runs frequently and pauses your program while it works, it has to be fast, and its design is built around the fact that most young objects are already dead. Recall that new space has two semi-spaces. Call them from-space and to-space. All allocation happens in the active one. When it fills up, the scavenger runs. It starts from the roots, which are the things that are obviously still in use: the stack, global variables, and a few other references. It follows every pointer from the roots, and each live object it finds is copied into the other semi-space, the to-space. Then the roles of the two semi-spaces swap. Everything left behind in the old one is garbage, and it is not even visited. The whole region is simply treated as empty.

That is the beautiful part. The cost of a scavenge depends on how many objects are alive, not on how many objects were allocated. If ninety-nine percent of the young objects are dead, the scavenger touches only one percent. Dead objects cost nothing. And as a side effect, the survivors end up packed together in memory with no gaps, which is good for cache behavior. Survivors are not copied forever. V8 uses an age mechanism: an object that has survived one scavenge is copied within the young generation, and an object that survives a second one is promoted, meaning moved to the old generation. This keeps long-lived objects out of the young space, so the scavenger does not keep copying them back and forth.

There is a subtlety. What if an old object holds a pointer to a young object? The scavenger only starts from the roots and walks the young generation, so it would miss that reference and wrongly free a live object. To solve this, V8 uses a write barrier. Whenever your code stores a pointer into an old object that points at a young one, the barrier records that location in a set of remembered slots. The scavenger treats those slots as additional roots. It is a small cost on stores, paid so that minor collections never have to scan the whole old generation.

Modern V8 scavenges in parallel. Several helper threads cooperate to copy objects, so the pause is shorter on multi-core machines. The scavenger is still a stop-the-world pause, but for a typical young generation it is usually brief, in the range of about a millisecond or a few. Let's verify some of this. Run `node --trace-gc gc.js` again and focus on the Scavenge lines. Count how often they happen and read the pause times. Now make the program keep every object it allocates, by pushing them into a global array. Run it again and watch what changes. The scavenges now copy much more, promote objects, and the old generation grows. That is your first look at how retention changes the behavior of the collector, and next we see what the old generation does when it fills up.

What does this teach us about how to write code? Short-lived allocation is cheap in V8. Creating a small object that dies a moment later costs a pointer bump and, eventually, almost nothing at scavenge time. So do not contort your code to avoid every temporary object. The cases that hurt are different: allocating in a very hot loop at a huge rate, so that scavenges run constantly, and creating objects that live just long enough to survive two scavenges, because those get copied twice and promoted, only to die in the old generation where cleanup is more costly. That second pattern has a name, mid-life crisis, and it is common in request handling code that caches results for a few seconds. If you see lots of promotion in the logs but the old generation does not stay big, that is a hint.

When the old generation grows large enough, V8 runs the major collector, which uses an algorithm called mark-sweep-compact. In the trace-gc output you will see these as Mark-Compact lines, sometimes also labeled with a reason like allocation failure or a finalize step for incremental marking. This is a heavier collection than a scavenge, because the old generation is big and its objects are mostly alive, so copying everything would be too expensive. Let's go through the three phases. First is marking. The collector starts from the roots again and walks through every reachable object, marking each one as live. Conceptually it colors objects: white means not yet seen, grey means seen but its children are not yet processed, and black means fully processed. When the walk ends, anything still white is unreachable, and so it is garbage. This is called tracing, and it means reference cycles are no problem. Two objects pointing at each other but unreachable from any root still get collected. That is a major difference from simple reference counting.

Second is sweeping. The collector goes through memory pages and turns the space occupied by unmarked objects into free blocks that can be reused for future allocation. It does not move anything. It just records the gaps. This is cheaper than copying, and V8 can do much of the sweeping concurrently with your program running. Third is compaction, which is optional. Over time sweeping leaves memory fragmented, with live objects scattered between small holes. If the fragmentation on some pages is high, V8 evacuates the live objects from those pages into other pages, tightening the layout and updating all pointers to the moved objects. Compaction is the most expensive phase, which is why V8 does it selectively, only where it pays off.

The big engineering story here is pause time. A long stop-the-world pause makes your page stutter or your server stall. So V8 has worked hard to take major collection work off the main thread. Marking can be done incrementally, in small slices interleaved with your code, and concurrently, on helper threads while JavaScript keeps running. Sweeping and parts of compaction also run in parallel or concurrently. The project that gathered these improvements is called Orinoco. The write barrier plays an even bigger role here, because it has to keep the marking correct while your code is changing objects.

Let's see it. Take `gc.js` and change it to retain a lot of data, say a growing array of objects, until memory reaches a few hundred megabytes. Run it with `node --trace-gc gc.js`. You will see scavenges at first, and later Mark-Compact lines with larger times. If your process dies with a heap out of memory error, try running with a higher `--max-old-space-size`, or better, find out why the data is retained. That last point is the general lesson. A garbage collector frees only what is unreachable. If you accidentally keep a reference, in a cache with no limit, a forgotten listener, or a closure holding a big object, it is a leak as far as V8 is concerned.

So we have the complete picture. Fast scavenges for the many short-lived objects, heavier but mostly concurrent mark-sweep-compact for the long-lived ones. In the final chapter we turn all of this knowledge into habits for writing code V8 likes. Let me tie the trace-gc output to what we just learned. A Mark-Compact line gives you the heap size before and after, the pause time, and often a note about the reason. If the time field is large but the main thread was barely blocked, much of the work was done concurrently, and the real pause is smaller than the total. For a precise view you can use the performance hooks module in Node, which can report garbage collection events with their durations, or the Chrome DevTools memory tools attached through `node --inspect`.

Finally, remember the connection to the earlier chapters. Object shapes affect memory too, since objects sharing a hidden class do not each carry their own copy of the layout description. And optimized code lives in memory that the collector manages as well. Everything in the engine shares one heap, and a healthy program is one that keeps that heap calm.

Welcome to the final chapter. Everything so far has been understanding. Now we turn it into habits. The first and most valuable habit comes straight from the inline cache lecture: keep your hot code monomorphic, or at worst a little polymorphic, and avoid megamorphic sites. Let me restate the three states, because they are the vocabulary of V8 performance. A call site or property access that has only ever seen one type or shape is monomorphic. One that has seen a few, up to about four, is polymorphic. One that has seen more is megamorphic. The same words apply to function calls: a call site that always calls the same function can be inlined, while one that calls many different functions cannot.

Let's measure the effect in a file called `mono.js`. I define `function area(shape) { return shape.w * shape.h; }`. In the first test I create a million objects all with the same literal, `{ w: 2, h: 3 }`, and call `area` on each in a loop. In the second test I make the objects with different shapes by adding different extra properties first, like `{ a: 1, w: 2, h: 3 }`, `{ b: 1, w: 2, h: 3 }`, and so on for eight kinds. Time both with `performance.now()`. On my machine the second is clearly slower, and the gap grows as I add shapes. Your numbers will differ, and that is fine, the direction is what matters.

Now let's turn that into rules. First, create objects of the same logical type the same way: same properties, same order, ideally initialized together in a constructor or a factory function. Second, do not add properties later in different places, since that spawns shape branches. Third, avoid `delete`, which can push an object into dictionary mode. Fourth, if a field may be absent, initialize it anyway with `null` rather than leaving it off, so the shape does not depend on the data. The same thinking applies to arrays. Keep arrays holding one kind of element where you can. An array of small integers is stored in a compact, fast form. If you push a floating point number, it transitions to a more general kind, and if you push a string or an object, it generalizes again. The transitions do not go back. Also avoid creating holes, for example by writing at an index far beyond the length, because holey arrays are slower than packed ones.

And functions? Keep the argument types of hot functions consistent. A function `add` that is always given two integers is much happier than one given integers, floats, strings and undefined over time. Avoid passing different numbers of arguments from different call sites to the same hot function, as that can force adaptation work. Now the important caveat. These are guidelines for hot code, the inner loops and the functions that profiling says matter. In most of your program none of this is visible. Do not make your code worse to read in order to save nanoseconds that nobody will notice. Measure first, and use these rules to understand what you measured. We will see how to find the hot code at the end of this chapter.

Next, we look at the specific things that make optimized code bail out. A final practical tip on this topic. Classes and constructors make shape consistency almost automatic, because every instance runs the same constructor body. Plain object literals built by hand in many different places are where drift creeps in, since each author adds fields in their own order. If you notice that your hot code handles records from many sources, consider a small factory function that builds them all, so that there is exactly one place that decides the layout.

In the TurboFan chapter we saw that deoptimization is the safety net. Now let's go through the common reasons optimized code gets thrown away, so that you can recognize them in `--trace-deopt` output. Run all of these experiments with `node --trace-opt --trace-deopt` and the right file. The first trigger is a type change. We have seen it with `deopt.js`: a function optimized for integers receives a string, and the guard fails. Closely related is a number representation change. If the function was optimized for small integers and then gets a floating point number, or an integer too large for the small integer range, the guard fails. The reason line mentions things like not a Smi or lost precision, depending on your version.

The second trigger is a shape change. If an optimized property load expected a particular hidden class and then sees an object with another one, the guard fails with a reason like wrong map. Modifying an object's shape after the optimized code was compiled can even invalidate the code lazily, without any failing guard, because the code registered a dependency on that shape. Third, out-of-bounds and holes. Reading beyond the end of an array, or reading a hole in an array, can fail the assumptions of the optimized element access. Fourth, insufficient type feedback: optimized code that reaches a branch which had never run before, so there was no feedback, will deoptimize there rather than guess. This is a very common one right after startup, and it is harmless if it happens once.

There are several others. Using `arguments` in unusual ways, calling a function with a different number of arguments than expected, certain uses of `try` and `catch` in older engines, and operations the compiler does not support well can all cause trouble. Many of these limitations have been removed as V8 has matured, which is why I do not want you to memorize a list. Memorize the method instead. The method is this. When you see a deopt in the trace, note the reason, then look at the exact function. Ask which assumption failed and who violated it. Fix the caller or make the data uniform. Then rerun and confirm the deopt is gone. This takes ten minutes once you have done it a couple of times.

Here is a worked example. In `deopt.js`, imagine the call that passes strings comes from a function that reads user input. The simplest fix is to convert the input to a number at the boundary, like `Number(input)`, so the hot function only ever sees numbers. We pushed the type uncertainty out to the edge, where it is cheap, and kept the hot core clean. That pattern, normalize at the boundary, is something you can apply almost anywhere. One more thing: do not try to prevent all deopts. A few during warm-up are normal. What you want to prevent is the loop, where a function is optimized and thrown away repeatedly. The trace shows it plainly, with the same function name appearing in alternating optimize and deopt lines. If you see that, you have found your problem.

Now we need a tool for finding the functions that matter in the first place, and that is profiling. It is also worth knowing that V8 remembers. If a function has been deoptimized many times, the engine becomes more conservative about optimizing it again, and the feedback it collected is broader after each round. So a function that is unlucky in its first minutes of life may settle into a good state later. This is why a long-running server and a short script can have very different profiles, and why you should test the behavior under realistic, warmed-up load rather than from a cold start.

We have spent a whole chapter on how to write code V8 likes, and I have kept saying measure first. This final lecture is how to measure. The tool is the V8 sampling profiler, which you turn on with the `--prof` flag. It periodically samples what the program is doing and writes the samples to a log, which you analyze afterwards. Create a file called `prof.js`. It should do some realistic work: for example, build an array of a few hundred thousand objects, then run a function that filters and sums them, and a function that formats strings. Make one function deliberately slow, say by passing mixed shapes into it. Now run `node --prof prof.js`. When it finishes, you will find a new file in the folder named like `isolate` followed by an address and `v8.log`. It can be large, and it is not meant for human eyes.

To read it, run `node --prof-process` followed by that log file name. The tool prints a report with several sections. The first is a summary, giving the number of ticks, where a tick is one sample, split into JavaScript, C++, garbage collection and other. That tells you quickly where the time went. Is it your code, the runtime, or the collector? A high GC share points back to our memory chapter, and a high C++ share often points at slow generic paths in the runtime.

Next come tables of the top functions, listed by ticks, for the JavaScript and C++ parts. Then the bottom up profile, which is the most useful section. It lists the heaviest functions and under each one, who called it. Find your slow function at the top, read its callers, and you know both what is slow and the path that leads to it. Names that start with an asterisk were running as optimized code, and a tilde marks interpreted code, which is a quick way to see which tier a hot function was in. Combine the tools now. Take the hot function from the profile, run `node --trace-opt --trace-deopt prof.js` and see whether it was optimized or kept bailing out. Print its bytecode with `--print-bytecode` if you want to understand what it does. Check its inputs for shape and type consistency. Make a change, and run the profile again to compare. That loop of measuring, forming a hypothesis from the pipeline, changing one thing and measuring again is the entire craft.

There is a more visual alternative. Node also supports `--cpu-prof`, which writes a `cpuprofile` file you can open in Chrome DevTools to see a flame chart. Many people find that easier than the text report. Use whichever you like. The principle is the same: let data point you at the few functions that deserve your attention. Let's wrap up the course. We started with source text and followed it through the scanner, the parser and the AST, into Ignition bytecode with its accumulator and feedback slots. We watched TurboFan speculate from that feedback and deoptimize when the speculation failed. We learned that hidden classes and inline caches make property access cheap when objects are consistent. We saw the heap split into young and old generations, with the scavenger and mark-sweep-compact keeping it clean. And we turned all of that into a few habits and a method.

I hope the engine feels less like a black box now. When something is fast or slow, you have a vocabulary to describe it and four flags to check it: `--print-bytecode`, `--trace-opt`, `--trace-deopt` and `--prof`. Keep experimenting with small files, expect details to change between V8 versions, and trust measurements over folklore. Thanks for following along, and happy hacking. Before you go, here is a small project for you to try on your own. Take any function in a codebase you know, put it in a file by itself with realistic input, and walk through the tools in order. Profile it with `--prof`, check its optimization history with the trace flags, read its bytecode, and then check object shapes with `%HaveSameMap` under `--allow-natives-syntax`. By the end you will have touched every stage of the pipeline on code you actually care about, and that is worth more than any lecture.
